title: Wine Yeast Engineering for Improved Polysaccharide Depolymerization and Lower Ethyl Carbamate Formation
content: Engineering wine yeasts to combine efficient extracellular polysaccharide degradation with reduced accumulation of ethyl carbamate, a group 2A carcinogen, may support improvements in winemaking. This study aimed to replace the arginase-encoding CAR1 locus in the genome of the triploid industrial wine yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae I-328 with an expression cassette for the endopolygalacturonase gene PGU1, placed under the control of the PGK1 gene promoter and terminator. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing was performed using an acetamidase-selectable plasmid followed by phenotypic screening and molecular genetic verification. Whole genome sequencing confirmed the replacement of all three CAR1 alleles by the PGU1 expression cassettes. The modified strain I328-Y21 showed enhanced degradation of polygalacturonic acid relative to the parental strain. Consistently, RT-qPCR analysis showed that the transcription level of the PGU1 gene in strain I328-Y21 was about 300 times higher than in I-328. Inactivation of arginase, which forms urea through the breakdown of arginine, resulted in about nine-fold decrease in the content of urea in the growth medium. Since ethyl carbamate is formed as a result of the interaction between ethanol and urea excreted by yeast cells, this strain could be used to reduce its content in wine. Winemaking experiments show that genome editing did not affect fermentation performance and other technological characteristics. The new strain with the replacement of the arginase gene with the endopolygalacturonase expression cassette is promising for use in winemaking.
